title: Casual Sex Is Linked to Lower Self-Esteem and Weaker Moral Orientations in Women But Not Men
author: Dolan, Eric W.
summary: Research in Personality and Individual Differences finds that unrestricted sociosexuality (willingness for casual sex outside relationships) correlates in women with lower self-esteem, reduced authenticity, weaker moral orientations, and higher moral disengagement—but shows no such correlation in men. The study raises an uncomfortable question: when a culture tells people decisions are freely chosen and consequence-free, yet data shows significant psychological costs, what is actually happening? The body registers what ideology denies, suggesting the gap between cultural narrative and lived psychic reality.
points: Casual sex outside relationships correlates with lower self-esteem and moral orientation in women but not men—a striking gender difference.
The research documents the gap between what culture promises (freedom without consequence) and what the body and psyche actually record.
Reduced authenticity and weaker moral orientations follow casual sex patterns in women, suggesting deep alignment between sexuality and identity.
Higher moral disengagement in women practicing casual sex suggests internalized conflict between behavior and values.
The body keeps biological and psychological score on choices ideology claims are consequence-free.
quotes: Unrestricted sociosexuality correlates in women, but not men, with lower self-esteem, reduced sense of authenticity, weaker moral orientations, and higher tendencies toward moral disengagement.

The finding raises a harder question that the researchers gesture toward without fully entering: what does it mean when the decisions a culture tells people are freely chosen and consequence-free turn out to be neither?
The data here is not about judgment. It is about the gap between what a culture promises and what the body and psyche actually record.
How a person's body records and responds to their choices is not incidental to flourishing—it is constitutive.” Archived from PsyPost on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
